title: Cell collectives pursue organ-level target morphologies despite perturbation

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Cell collectives pursue organ-level target morphologies despite perturbation

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Regulative development and regeneration (e.g. scrambled tadpole faces that still become normal frog faces, tail grafts remodelling into limbs, kidney tubules of constant diameter despite enlarged cells) show that somatic cells pursue specific target morphologies despite perturbation, with set points that are large organ-level macrostates not defined at the single-cell level.

fields.label: Work
fields.value: The Computational Boundary of a "Self": Developmental Bioelectricity Drives Multicellularity and Scale-Free Cognition

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Levin M 2019, The Computational Boundary of a "Self": Developmental Bioelectricity Drives Multicellularity and Scale-Free Cognition › Body Patterning and Cognition: A Common Origin

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: They reveal the ability of somatic cells to not only pursue specific target morphologies despite perturbations and novel scenarios, but to pursue collective patterning outcomes that are truly enormous with respect to the scale of size and organization of single cells

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Levin M, “The Computational Boundary of a "Self": Developmental Bioelectricity Drives Multicellularity and Scale-Free Cognition”, Frontiers in psychology (2019), doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2019.02688; section “Body Patterning and Cognition: A Common Origin”. Scope: Regulative development and regeneration in vertebrates (Xenopus, salamanders, axolotls, newts)

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on levin-2019-boundary-03: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.54

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Return toward organ-level morphology is measurable and existing studies cover several examples. The stronger language of pursuing a target macrostate is not uniquely distinguished from distributed local rules, and available data cover only a subset of the stated generalization.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: For public regeneration and regulative-development series, quantify convergence toward a reference organ morphology after perturbation and compare collective correction with local cell-autonomous or passive-mechanical models.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Target pursuit is an interpretation of morphological convergence.

Named examples span species and incompatible measurements.

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: A set point is operationalized here as restoration of organ geometry after perturbation, which is a real measurement. The cited Xenopus, salamander, and tubule results were published as measurements and can be compiled for a subset of the scope. They are not one downloadable morphometric table, and a local developmental program predicts the same restorations. Existing literature can pressure the claim on those examples and cannot settle the cognitive wording or the full vertebrate scope.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: After a defined perturbation (scrambled craniofacial primordia, a tail graft, or an enlarged tubule cell), measure whether the collective returns to the species-typical organ geometry rather than to a locally stable wrong shape. Return to the target supports a large-scale set point; stable wrong anatomies after the same perturbations would refute it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Return to normal shape is also predicted by local gene-regulatory programs.

The classic cases are spread across papers and taxa, with no shared landmark file.

Kidney-tubule and salamander graft results are not in Xenbase.
